- **Organizer:** Since AI is a Finnish nonprofit organisation, founded by a team of students from the University of Turku.
- **Background:** The inaugural Since AI Hackathon in 2025 brought together 260 builders who shipped more than 30 AI projects.
- **Applying:** Sign-up is through sinceai.app, with more information at sinceai.ai/hackathon.

content.text:
The starter repo is set up in `/data/dev/sinceAI_hackathon`. Tests pass, the Docker image builds, and the files are staged in git but not committed or pushed yet.

**The event:** Since AI Hackathon 2026 is in Turku, Finland (EduCity, Turku University of Applied Sciences), from 6 to 8 November. It runs 72 hours, with challenges from about 15 companies and a €50k cash prize pool. Teams can have up to 5 people, so your team is the maximum size. You won't know the challenge until kickoff, so the repo is general-purpose and easy to adapt.

**What each file is for:**

| File | Plain-English purpose |
|---|---|
| [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml) + `uv.lock` | Lists the Python libraries. `uv` installs them, and the lock file means all 5 of you get exactly the same versions. |
| [.python-version](.python-version) | Pins everyone to Python 3.12. |
| [app/main.py](app/main.py) | The backend server (FastAPI). It has one test endpoint, `/health`, and your real code goes here. |
| [app/config.py](app/config.py) | Reads settings and API keys from `.env`. |
| [app/ui.py](app/ui.py) | A tiny web page (Streamlit) for showing the project to the judges. You can drop it if you build a real frontend. |
| [tests/](tests/) | Automatic checks that the code still works. |
| [Dockerfile](Dockerfile) / [compose.yaml](compose.yaml) | Run the backend and UI in Docker with one command, so it behaves the same on every laptop. There's a commented-out database you can switch on if you need one. |
| [.env.example](.env.example) | A template for secret keys. Each person copies it to `.env`, which git ignores so keys never get committed. |
| [.gitignore](.gitignore) / [.dockerignore](.dockerignore) | Keep junk and secrets out of git and out of the Docker image. |
| [Makefile](Makefile) | Short commands: `make setup`, `make dev`, `make ui`, `make test`, `make fmt`, `make up`. |
| [.pre-commit-config.yaml](.pre-commit-config.yaml) | Before every commit, tidies the code and blocks private keys and big files. |
| [.github/workflows/ci.yml](.github/workflows/ci.yml) | GitHub runs the lint check and tests on every push, so a broken `main` shows up fast. |
| [.github/pull_request_template.md](.github/pull_request_template.md) / [.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/task.md](.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/task.md) | Simple forms for pull requests and tasks, so 5 people stay organised. |
| [docs/PLAN.md](docs/PLAN.md) | Suggested roles for 5 people, a 72-hour timeline and team rules. |
| [docs/PITCH.md](docs/PITCH.md) | An outline for the final pitch, which counts for a lot at hackathons. |
| `data/`, `notebooks/` | Local data (not committed) and space for experiments. |

**What else I'd add before Friday:**
1. **A GitHub org or private repo** with all 5 of you added. I can commit this and create it with `gh` if you'd like.
2. **LLM API keys** sorted out in advance, plus any credits the event or its sponsors offer.
3. **Somewhere to deploy the demo**, such as Fly.io, Railway or a cheap server, so judges can try a live URL. Record a backup demo video as well.
4. **A GitHub Projects board** (To do / Doing / Done) for the tasks.
5. **Have everyone run `make setup` before the event** so no one loses hours to install problems on day one.

- [University of Turku event page](https://www.utu.fi/en/news/events/since-ai-hackathon-2026-1000-ai-builders-coming-to-turku)
- [Luma listing](https://luma.com/b01ucdc9)

# Running on LUMI (AMD MI250X GPUs, ROCm)

LUMI has **no Docker** and its GPUs are **AMD** -> we use LUMI's prebuilt
PyTorch+ROCm Singularity container and add our other deps on top with uv.

## One-time setup (on a LUMI login node)
```bash
export PROJECT=project_XXXXXXXXX          # <- our LUMI project id
cd /scratch/$PROJECT/$USER
git clone <repo-url> sinceai && cd sinceai
bash lumi/setup.sh
```

## Run a job
```bash
sbatch lumi/train.sbatch          # edit the command at the bottom
squeue --me                       # check queue
tail -f logs/*.out
```

## Quick interactive GPU shell (debugging)
```bash
srun -p small-g --gpus-per-node=1 -t 00:30:00 -A $PROJECT --pty \
  singularity exec $SIF bash -c 'source .venv-lumi/bin/activate && python'
```

## Notes
- Put data/models in `/scratch/$PROJECT` or `/flash/$PROJECT`, NOT `$HOME` (tiny quota).
- 1 MI250X = 2 GCDs; Slurm/PyTorch see **8 "GPUs" per node** (`--gpus-per-node=8`).
- Set `HF_HOME` to scratch so model downloads don't fill `$HOME`.
- In code, `torch.cuda.*` works as normal on ROCm (`device="cuda"`).
- Container list: `ls /appl/local/containers/sif-images/`
  (pick the newest `lumi-pytorch-rocm-*.sif` and set it in `lumi/env.sh`).
EOF

export HF_HOME=/scratch/$PROJECT/$USER/hf_cache
export UV_CACHE_DIR=/scratch/$PROJECT/$USER/uv_cache
export SINGULARITY_BIND=/scratch/$PROJECT,/flash/$PROJECT,/appl/local/containers

EOF

#!/bin/bash
# Creates .venv-lumi on top of the container's torch (no torch reinstall).
set -euo pipefail
source "$(dirname "$0")/env.sh"
mkdir -p logs "$HF_HOME"
singularity exec "$SIF" bash -c '
  python -m venv --system-site-packages .venv-lumi
  source .venv-lumi/bin/activate

  uv export --no-hashes --group ml --no-dev --no-emit-project \

content.text:
Everything now runs on GPU, and nothing is committed or pushed.

**Why Python 3.12:** it's the safest version for an ML stack. PyTorch, transformers and the LUMI containers all support it well, whereas newer versions sometimes lack wheels for libraries you might grab mid-hackathon. I've now pinned it to 3.12 only, so all 5 of you get identical environments.

**What I added (all in `pyproject.toml`):**
- **Always installed:** `anthropic` and `openai` for LLM APIs, plus `numpy`, `pandas`, `polars`, `scikit-learn`, `matplotlib` and `tqdm`.
- **`ml` group:** `transformers`, `sentence-transformers`, `accelerate` and `datasets`.
- **PyTorch as a choice of builds:** `make setup` installs the NVIDIA GPU build by default, and `make setup TORCH=cpu` is there for anyone without a GPU. torchaudio is out because the current GPU builds don't have a matching wheel.
- **GPU check:** I tested it on your RTX 4050 with `uv run python -m app.train`, and it found the GPU and ran on it. Tests pass.
- **Docker** builds the GPU version by default and passes the GPU into the container. The host needs `nvidia-container-toolkit` for that. I didn't rebuild the GPU image because it's very large.

**LUMI:** its GPUs are AMD MI250X, which need a different PyTorch build (ROCm) from NVIDIA cards, and LUMI has no Docker. The plain pip ROCm builds would also likely clash with LUMI's drivers. So the new `lumi/` folder uses LUMI's own prebuilt PyTorch container instead:
- `lumi/setup.sh` adds your other libraries on top of the container's PyTorch.
- `lumi/train.sbatch` is a job script you submit to LUMI's job queue.
- `lumi/README.md` has the instructions.

I couldn't test any of the LUMI part because I don't have access. Replace `project_XXXXXXXXX` with your LUMI project ID, and run `lumi/setup.sh` before Friday to catch problems early.

**On not writing code before Friday:** check the official rules (sinceai.ai/hackathon) or ask the organisers. Most hackathons forbid writing the actual project in advance but allow general boilerplate, and this repo has nothing challenge-specific in it, only setup. Your plan works:
1. Keep it local until Friday. The folder has a git repo but no commits yet.
2. Get everyone's install working now, since installing the GPU libraries takes a while.
3. On Friday: `git commit`, create the GitHub repo, push, and add your teammates.

If the rules turn out to be strict, you can say at kickoff that the repo contains only setup.

Most AI hackathons allow pre-existing code only under strict conditions, and the rules vary a lot by event:

- **Disclosure and extension are common.** The Build with AI: Transforming Personal Finance hackathon requires you to disclose all information about pre-existing code in your submission and to fork your repository so it's clear which code is new. The TMLS Agentic Hackathon lets teams use prior work or existing repositories as a starting point, but it must be clearly disclosed in the submission form.
- **New work must dominate.** The AI Tinkerers Abu Dhabi rules say submissions must be net new code or functionality created during the hackathon, though you can extend an existing repo if you build substantial new features.
- **Some events ban prior projects outright.** AI Tinkerers Portland's Secure Agents Buildathon says pre-built products or previously completed projects are not eligible. The SUST CSE Carnival rulebook excludes projects developed, even partially, before the hackathon begins.
- **Some allow it with lineage requirements.** ETH Bishkek permits an existing project only if it was born at another hackathon and all previous iterations of the same project at previous hackathons must be linked in the submission. It also says teams must not create a new repository and "single commit" all their code.
- **Commit timing matters.** At DEVCUP, code committed before the hackathon begins would not be considered for evaluation.

Judging also tends to favor new work. The Build with AI rules note that projects that use a majority of pre-existing work historically do not score as high in judging.

I ran one search, so these examples come from a handful of events rather than a complete survey. For a specific hackathon, check its official rules page or handbook for the exact policy.

content.text:
Good news: the rules allow pre-existing code. You just have to keep it separate from what you build at the event and say so.

**What the rules say** ([Builder Guide](https://sinceai.ai/hackathon-2026/guide/builders), [Field Guide](https://sinceai.ai/hackathon-2026/guide)):
- **Pre-existing code:** "Separate pre-existing code and assets from what you built at the event." Neither guide says anything about templates or git history, and neither uses the word "disqualification".
- **Preparing ahead is encouraged:** "Download your programming tools, dependencies, container images and AI models in advance."
- **Building starts Friday at 19:30**, when the full challenge materials open in sinceai.app. Challenge summaries open Thursday 5 Nov at 15:00, so read them then.
- **Repository:**
  - "Commit often with meaningful messages; keep a README with reproducible setup steps."
  - A private repo is fine only if the judges can open it.
  - ZIP files aren't accepted.
  - Never commit secrets.
- **Submission:**
  - Deadline is Sunday 8 Nov at 10:00, through sinceai.app.
  - You give a repo or demo link and a "Built with" list.
  - You must disclose the GenAI tools you used.
  - Every member accepts the challenge's IP terms, and every member must check in in person on Friday.
- **Working demo required:** "No mockups. Working demos first."

**LUMI may be a problem:** the deadline to register for LUMI/CSC access was **Friday 30 October**, and nobody can join the hackathon's LUMI project after it. Accounts also need a personal institutional email from an EU or Horizon-associated organisation. If your team didn't register, LUMI is probably off the table. Check for the 25 October email with "SUPERCOMPUTER" in the subject, or ask info@sinceai.fi. Without LUMI, your RTX 4050 and the `cuda` setup still work.

**Timestamps:**
- `git init` records no date, and neither does staging files. Git doesn't store file creation times either.
- Each commit is stamped with your computer's clock at the moment you run `git commit`. The GitHub repo's creation date is when you create it on GitHub.
- So if you first commit on Friday, the whole history starts on Friday.
- Commit dates can easily be faked, though, so judges don't treat them as proof of anything. Being upfront counts for more.

**My recommendation:** there's no need to hide anything, since the rules allow pre-existing code. On Friday, make the first commit "Pre-event boilerplate" and build everything after it. I added a "Pre-existing work" section to the README saying exactly that, plus a "GenAI tools used" section for the submission form. That separation is what the rules ask for.

"""One-liner LLM helpers. Usage:
    from app.llm import ask
    ask("Summarise this: ...")                 # Claude by default
    ask("...", provider="openai")
    ask("...", system="You are a JSON API.")
"""
from typing import Literal

from app.config import settings

Provider = Literal["anthropic", "openai"]


def ask(prompt: str, system: str = "", provider: Provider = "anthropic", max_tokens: int = 2048) -> str:
    if provider == "anthropic":
        import anthropic

        client = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key=settings.anthropic_api_key)
        msg = client.messages.create(
            model=settings.anthropic_model,
            max_tokens=max_tokens,
            system=system or anthropic.NOT_GIVEN,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        )
        return "".join(b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text")

    from openai import OpenAI

    client = OpenAI(api_key=settings.openai_api_key)
    messages = ([{"role": "system", "content": system}] if system else []) + [
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
    ]
    r = client.chat.completions.create(model=settings.openai_model, messages=messages)
    return r.choices[0].message.content or ""


def embed(texts: list[str], model: str = "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"):

    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

    return SentenceTransformer(model).encode(texts, normalize_embeddings=True)

// building & submissions

Build with AI. Submit in sinceai.app.
What you can use, what you stay responsible for, and exactly how your team submits by Sunday 8 November, 10:00 EET.

AI tools · permitted and encouraged

Build with AI. We encourage it.
Use the best tools available to turn real problems into working solutions — and be ready to explain, demonstrate and stand behind what you build.

ChatGPT
Claude and Claude Code
Google Gemini
GitHub Copilot
Cursor
Lovable
OpenCode
…or any other AI assistant, coding agent, model, framework or developer platform.

AI is a choice, not a requirement — you don't need a paid subscription to compete.

Your team stays responsible
—
Understand your solution and verify generated code — you are responsible for its security, reliability and behaviour.
—
Be ready to explain your engineering decisions.
—
Disclose the main AI tools you used — the submission form asks. No need to label AI-written lines.
—
Separate pre-existing code and assets from what you built at the event.
—
Licences, the challenge's rules and its data restrictions still apply.
Partner tools and benefits: computing, AI models, app builders and developer tools from our technology partners, with quickstarts and where to get help, in AI Tools & Resources.

How to submit your project
Official platform

sinceai.app

The official submission platform is sinceai.app, not Devpost. An entry on Devpost alone is not a submission.

Deadline · fixed

Sunday 8 November, 10:00 EET

On your sinceai.app dashboard, the event card shows Submit project while submissions are open (Edit submission once you have submitted).

Required
Challenge
Your team's Friday selection, filled in for you; only the organisers can change it.
Project name
Up to 80 characters.
Tagline
One sentence on what your project does, up to 140 characters. Voters read it first on every vote card.
About the project
The problem, your solution, how you built it, what you met on the way and what comes next — up to 5,000 characters. Judges read all of it; voters see the first lines.
Built with
Technologies you used, comma-separated. The first five appear as chips on your vote card.
Repository
A link to your code, public or private. If it is private, judges use your source-code .zip.
Demo video
A public or unlisted YouTube link, ideally under two minutes. YouTube is the only accepted format — no video file uploads.
Source code
One .zip of your code as it stands at the deadline, up to 100 MB.
MLH questions
Technology feedback, the GenAI tools you used (or “I did not use GenAI”) and whether you implemented a generative AI model or API.
Challenge terms
Accepted by submitting. On a challenge that transfers ownership, every team member ticks them personally first.
Public summary (confidential challenges only)
A public-safe summary, and your confirmation that the project name, tagline, summary and Built with contain no confidential data.
What is confidential
Optional
Demo URL
A link where your project can be tried, if it is deployed. Judges see it; voters don't.
Pitch deck
One PDF or PowerPoint. Voters can open it from your vote card.
Supporting documents
Up to two, for the judges.
Partner technologies
Tick the partner technologies you used and say how in a sentence or two. Ticking Red Hat OpenShift AI or FIWARE also enters that award, with the evidence it asks for.
Optional awards
MLH prize categories
Tick the MLH categories that fit — zero, one or several.
Optional awards
Domain name and schools of team members
Optional MLH questions.
Gemini API project number
Leave it blank unless a prize category you enter asks for it.
Files
Source code
Required
ZIP
One file, up to 100 MB. Leave out dependencies such as node_modules, and data files.
Pitch deck
Optional
PDF, PPT, PPTX
One file.
Supporting documents
Optional
PDF, PPT, PPTX, DOC, DOCX, TXT, Markdown
Up to two.
Demo video
Required
YouTube link
Public or unlisted. No MP4 or WebM uploads.
Files can be added before your first submit and are saved with it. The upload form shows the other size limits.

What voters see
One vote card, the same for every challenge, top to bottom:

1 Project
Challenge, project name and team.
2 Tagline
Your one sentence, in full.
3 Description
The first few lines of About the project, with Read more.
4 Demo video
Your YouTube video, playable on the card. Voters can vote without watching to the end.
5 Pitch deck
When you added one.
6 Built with
The first five technologies, as small chips.
Never on the card: your repository, your demo URL or other links. Voters compare about 20 pairs quickly and don't clone or deploy anything; judges and organisers still see your links.
Confidential (NDA) challenges get the same card, with only what your team confirmed public-safe: the project name, tagline, public summary and Built with — and the video and deck unless the company has turned them off. Until you confirm, voters see a neutral placeholder. The card shows no confidentiality label.
Step 1

Prepare the details
Write the tagline and description, list your Built with and keep your repository up to date while you build — not at 09:50 on Sunday.

Step 2

Upload your demo video to YouTube
Record a short demo, ideally under two minutes, and upload it as public or unlisted. Open the link logged out to check it plays.

Step 3

Zip your source code
One .zip, up to 100 MB, without node_modules or data files. Judges use it if your repository or demo can't be opened.

Step 4

Fill in the form and add files
Any team member submits — one entry per team. Add the zip, and a pitch deck if you have one, in the same go.

Step 5

Everyone accepts the terms
On a challenge that transfers ownership, each team member ticks the challenge terms for their own work — do it as soon as your team has its challenge.

Step 6

Check before 10:00
Review the entry, the video and every file. You can edit until submissions close.

Optional awards: on the same submission, tick MLH categories, and tick Red Hat OpenShift AI or FIWARE under Partner technologies to enter those awards — how to enter the optional awards.

What makes a strong entry
—
A working prototype — the product is the pitch.
—
A tagline a voter understands in five seconds.
—
A demo video that shows it working in the first 20 seconds, under two minutes in all.
—
A repository with a README and setup instructions.
—
A concise deck only if it helps; it never replaces a working prototype.

content.text: Turning your calendar into a live dashboard page; publishing it now.

I made a live board from your calendar file (`since-ai-hackathon-2026-builders.ics`, 35 events): https://claude.ai/artifact/7MfMoApJJotTFZzFQcsV2e

It shows Turku time and a big countdown to the next key moment, which right now is "Challenge summaries open" tomorrow at 15:00. It also lists what's happening now and the next 5 events, then the full schedule by day with past events faded and deadlines marked. There are two checklists, "Claim before Friday" and "Team prep". Ticks are saved in your browser only, so each teammate has their own. The page is private to you until you share it from claude.ai. A copy is in the repo at `docs/live.html`.

**Worth claiming now, in order:**
1. **Featherless AI, $25 credit:** every participant, no card needed, and the guide says to claim early. It gives you an API for open-weight models, which saves your own API credit.
2. **Google AI Pro + AI Studio ($10 a month of credit):** free for students for a year via MLH. The Gemini API is a solid second option next to Claude, and MLH has a Gemini prize category.
3. **Google Cloud, $300 trial:** a backup for GPUs and hosting if LUMI doesn't come through. Only one person needs to claim it.
4. **GitHub Copilot Student:** if anyone on the team is a verified student.
5. **n8n Cloud Pro:** one per team, so pick one person to claim it. Agree who before Friday.
6. **Pruna AI:** a shared team key for image and video generation. Only take it if the challenge involves images or video.
7. **Lovable Pro and ElevenLabs:** each is a free month that starts the moment you claim it, so claim them on Friday rather than now. Lovable is handy for building a quick frontend, and ElevenLabs is only worth it if voice is part of the challenge.
8. **Red Hat OpenShift Sandbox:** only if you're going for the Red Hat award, and it has to be set up before the event.

**Things in the guide that change our plan:**
- **Demo video:** a YouTube link is required, ideally under 2 minutes. It plays on every vote card, and the vote decides which 5 teams reach the finals. Show the project working within the first 20 seconds. This matters as much as the code.
- **Source code ZIP:** required, up to 100 MB, without data files or dependency folders. I'll add a `make zip` command tomorrow.
- **Tagline:** 140 characters or fewer, and voters read it first.
- **Q&A with the companies:** Saturday 09:00–12:00 and 14:30–18:00 at Joki. Show them an early version on Saturday morning.
- **FORCIT challenge:** the prize is bigger (€3,000 for first), but it requires signing an NDA on Friday.

I couldn't add the schedule to your Google Calendar because the Google Calendar connector isn't authorised; you'd need to connect it in your claude.ai connector settings. You can also import the `.ics` file directly into any calendar app.

"""One-liner LLM helpers for every provider we have keys for.

    from app.llm import ask, embed
    ask("Summarise this: ...")                       # uses LLM_PROVIDER from .env
    ask("...", provider="gemini")                    # anthropic | openai | featherless | gemini
    ask("...", provider="featherless", model="meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct")
    ask("...", system="Reply only with JSON.")

from functools import cache

from app.config import settings

# OpenAI-compatible providers: name -> (base_url, key attr, default model attr)
OPENAI_COMPAT = {
    "openai": (None, "openai_api_key", "openai_model"),
    "featherless": ("https://api.featherless.ai/v1", "featherless_api_key", "featherless_model"),
    "gemini": (

        "gemini_api_key",
        "gemini_model",
    ),
}
PROVIDERS = ["anthropic", *OPENAI_COMPAT]


@cache
def _openai_client(provider: str):
    from openai import OpenAI

    base_url, key_attr, _ = OPENAI_COMPAT[provider]
    return OpenAI(api_key=REDACTED, key_attr), base_url=base_url)


@cache
def _anthropic_client():
    import anthropic

    return anthropic.Anthropic(api_key=REDACTED


def ask(
    prompt: str,
    system: str = "",
    provider: str | None = None,
    model: str | None = None,
    max_tokens: int = 2048,
) -> str:
    provider = provider or settings.llm_provider
    if provider == "anthropic":
        import anthropic

        msg = _anthropic_client().messages.create(
            model=model or settings.anthropic_model,
            max_tokens=max_tokens,
            system=system or anthropic.NOT_GIVEN,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        )
        return "".join(b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text")

    if provider not in OPENAI_COMPAT:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown provider {provider!r}, pick one of {PROVIDERS}")
    messages = ([{"role": "system", "content": system}] if system else []) + [
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
    ]
    r = _openai_client(provider).chat.completions.create(
        model=model or getattr(settings, OPENAI_COMPAT[provider][2]),
        messages=messages,
        max_tokens=max_tokens,
    )
    return r.choices[0].message.content or ""


def list_models(provider: str) -> list[str]:
    if provider == "anthropic":
        return [m.id for m in _anthropic_client().models.list()]
    return sorted(m.id for m in _openai_client(provider).models.list())

def _st(model: str):
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

    return SentenceTransformer(model)


def embed(texts: list[str], model: str = "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"):
    """Local embeddings (GPU if available). Returns a normalised numpy array."""
    return _st(model).encode(texts, normalize_embeddings=True)

There are two kinds of models in the repo, and they work differently.

**1. API models: nothing to download**

These run on the company's servers. Your code sends text over the internet and gets an answer back, which is what `ask()` does. They're the big, smart models.

| Provider | Default model | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Anthropic | `claude-sonnet-5-5` | Strongest overall: reasoning, code, analysing documents |
| OpenAI | `gpt-5-mini` | A cheap, fast all-rounder |
| Gemini | `gemini-flash-latest` | Fast and cheap, good with images, MLH prize category |
| Featherless | `Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` | Open-source models, paid from the $25 credit |

You only need a key for these, and you only pay per use. You switch between them by changing `LLM_PROVIDER` in `.env`.

**2. Local models: downloaded with `make models`**

These are files saved to your laptop, around 10 GB in total, that run on your RTX 4050. That's why you download them at home: the venue Wi-Fi is shared. They're smaller, specialised tools rather than chatbots:

| Model | What it does | Example use |
|---|---|---|
| `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (~90 MB) | Turns text into numbers ("embeddings") so you can find similar text | Search over a company's documents |
| `bge-m3` (~2 GB) | The same, but stronger and understands Finnish | Several of the companies are Finnish, and their data may be in Finnish |
| `whisper-small` (~1 GB) | Speech to text | If a challenge involves audio, calls or meetings |
| `Qwen3-4B` (~8 GB, switched off) | A small chatbot that runs offline | Only if a company forbids sending its data to outside APIs |

Embeddings come from the `embed()` helper. Whisper and Qwen don't have helper functions yet; you'd call them with the `transformers` library.

**How they fit together:** a typical hackathon AI project is "**RAG**" (retrieval-augmented generation):
1. Split the company's documents into pieces and turn them into embeddings with a local model like `bge-m3`. This is fast, free, and the data never leaves your laptop.
2. When a user asks something, find the most relevant pieces.
3. Send those pieces plus the question to an API model like Claude, which writes the answer.

**What to actually download tonight:** MiniLM and bge-m3 for sure, since they're small and almost always useful. Add Whisper if you have the disk space. """Generic PyTorch training template (pre-event boilerplate).

At the event, replace the three TODO parts: `build_data`, `build_model`, `loss_and_metric`.
Everything else (GPU, mixed precision, checkpoints, TensorBoard, early stopping) is done.

    make train                               # or: uv run python -m app.train --epochs 20
    make tb                                  # watch curves at http://localhost:6006
Runs on NVIDIA (CUDA), LUMI (ROCm), Apple (MPS) or CPU.
"""

import argparse
import json
import random
import time
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset, random_split
from torch.utils.tensorboard import SummaryWriter


@dataclass
class Config:
    epochs: int = 10
    batch_size: int = 64
    lr: float = 3e-4
    weight_decay: float = 0.01
    val_frac: float = 0.15
    patience: int = 5  # early stopping: epochs without improvement
    seed: int = 42
    workers: int = 2
    run_name: str = ""


def pick_device() -> torch.device:
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        return torch.device("cuda")  # NVIDIA *and* AMD/ROCm (LUMI)
    if torch.backends.mps.is_available():
        return torch.device("mps")
    return torch.device("cpu")


def seed_everything(seed: int) -> None:
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- TODO 1: data
def build_data(cfg: Config):
    """Return (train_dataset, val_dataset). Dummy data: 2-class toy problem."""
    x = torch.randn(5000, 32)
    y = (x[:, :4].sum(dim=1) > 0).long()
    ds = TensorDataset(x, y)
    n_val = int(len(ds) * cfg.val_frac)
    return random_split(ds, [len(ds) - n_val, n_val])


# --------------------------------------------------------------- TODO 2: model
def build_model() -> nn.Module:
    """E.g. timm.create_model('efficientnet_b0', pretrained=True, num_classes=N)
    or AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(...)."""
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(32, 128), nn.GELU(), nn.Dropout(0.1), nn.Linear(128, 2))


# ------------------------------------------------------- TODO 3: loss + metric
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()


def loss_and_metric(model: nn.Module, batch, device) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, float]:
    x, y = (t.to(device, non_blocking=True) for t in batch)
    logits = model(x)
    acc = (logits.argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()
    return loss_fn(logits, y), acc  # metric: higher is better


# ------------------------------------------------------------- training loop
def run_epoch(model, loader, device, opt=None, sched=None, amp_dtype=None):
    train = opt is not None
    model.train(train)
    tot_loss = tot_metric = n = 0
    for batch in loader:
        with torch.set_grad_enabled(train), torch.autocast(
            device.type, dtype=amp_dtype, enabled=amp_dtype is not None
        ):
            loss, metric = loss_and_metric(model, batch, device)
        if train:
            opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            loss.backward()
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
            opt.step()
            sched.step()
        bs = len(batch[0])
        tot_loss += loss.item() * bs
        tot_metric += metric * bs
        n += bs
    return tot_loss / n, tot_metric / n


def main(cfg: Config) -> None:
    seed_everything(cfg.seed)
    device = pick_device()
    # bf16 mixed precision on modern GPUs (RTX 30xx/40xx, MI250X): ~2x faster, less memory
    amp_dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device.type == "cuda" and torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported() else None
    run = cfg.run_name or time.strftime("%m%d-%H%M%S")
    out = Path("runs") / run
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    (out / "config.json").write_text(json.dumps(asdict(cfg), indent=2))
    tb = SummaryWriter(out)
    print(f"device={device} amp={amp_dtype} -> {out}")

    train_ds, val_ds = build_data(cfg)
    kw = dict(batch_size=cfg.batch_size, num_workers=cfg.workers, pin_memory=device.type == "cuda")
    train_dl = DataLoader(train_ds, shuffle=True, drop_last=True, **kw)
    val_dl = DataLoader(val_ds, **kw)

    model = build_model().to(device)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=cfg.lr, weight_decay=cfg.weight_decay)
    sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(
        opt, max_lr=cfg.lr, total_steps=cfg.epochs * len(train_dl)
    )

    best, bad = -float("inf"), 0
    for ep in range(1, cfg.epochs + 1):
        t0 = time.time()
        tr_loss, tr_m = run_epoch(model, train_dl, device, opt, sched, amp_dtype)
        va_loss, va_m = run_epoch(model, val_dl, device, amp_dtype=amp_dtype)
        for k, v in dict(loss_train=tr_loss, loss_val=va_loss, m_train=tr_m, m_val=va_m).items():
            tb.add_scalar(k, v, ep)
        flag = ""
        if va_m > best:
            best, bad, flag = va_m, 0, " *best*"
            torch.save(model.state_dict(), out / "best.pt")
        else:
            bad += 1
        print(
            f"ep {ep:3d} | train {tr_loss:.4f}/{tr_m:.4f} | val {va_loss:.4f}/{va_m:.4f}"
            f" | {time.time() - t0:.1f}s{flag}"
        )
        if bad >= cfg.patience:
            print("early stop")
            break
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), out / "last.pt")
    (out / "result.json").write_text(json.dumps({"best_val_metric": best}, indent=2))
    print(f"best val metric {best:.4f} -> {out / 'best.pt'}")


def parse() -> Config:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    for k, v in asdict(Config()).items():
        p.add_argument(f"--{k.replace('_', '-')}", type=type(v), default=v)
    return Config(**{k.replace("-", "_"): v for k, v in vars(p.parse_args()).items()})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(parse())

Yes, that's a strong idea, and **Traficom is the best fit by far**, because radio signals follow well-known physics. It could also make your project stand out, since many teams will probably just wrap an LLM.

**How it would work for Traficom**
1. **Simulate:** generate thousands of scenarios with satellite and ground transmitters, different frequencies, power levels, distances and terrain. Physics formulas such as path loss and antenna patterns give the resulting signal and interference level.
2. **Train:** teach a model to go from a scenario to its interference risk.
3. **Use:** the model answers almost instantly, so a specialist can test thousands of frequency plans. A full physics simulation could be far too slow for that.
4. **Check:** test it against the simulator on scenarios it hasn't seen, and against any real data Traficom gives you.

This is called a **surrogate model**: a fast ML copy of a slow simulation. The demo is easy to follow too: a map showing an interference heatmap that updates live as you move a transmitter or change its frequency.

**How it fits your other picks**

| Challenge | Fit | What you'd simulate |
|---|---|---|
| **Traficom** | Strong | Radio propagation and interference |
| **Turku Energia** | Partial | Wind and solar output from weather, but market prices aren't physics |
| **Business Turku** | Good | Machine vibration and wear, to create fault examples that are rare in real data |
| **Europress** | Partial | Equipment faults, if the real signals are too few or unlabelled |
| **FORCIT** | Unknown | Possibly blast physics, but that can't be judged before the NDA briefing |

**The main risks**
- **It may only learn your simulator:** if the simulator is too simple, the model looks great but fails on real data. Ideally, train on simulated data and then test or fine-tune on real data.
- **The physics has to be right:** someone needs to own it, because specialists will spot mistakes quickly. You can reuse existing tools and published propagation models rather than writing everything from scratch.
- **It might be pointless:** if a formula alone solves the problem quickly, the ML adds little. Your pitch has to show where the model is faster or copes with something the simple formula can't.
- **Time:** you have about 38 hours. Keep the simulator simple, and get the whole pipeline working by Saturday morning.

**My recommendation:** this idea moves Traficom up to **first choice** if your team is excited by it, with Turku Energia as your backup. Then ask Traficom on Friday what real data they have, and which part of their current work is slowest.

We don't know exactly which signals yet, because the summary only says satellite and ground radio systems share spectrum. Here's what I'd expect, and how I'd solve it. Full details come at the Friday briefing.

## What "signal" probably means
**Radio transmissions:** energy sent at a set frequency, power and direction. Interference happens when one system's signal is strong enough at another system's receiver to disturb it.

| Likely system | Example | Role in a clash |
|---|---|---|
| **Satellite** | Earth stations, satellite TV and data, GPS/GNSS | Usually the victim, as signals from space arrive very weak |
| **Ground (terrestrial)** | 5G/mobile masts, microwave links, broadcast | Often the source, as it's close and strong |

**The data may not be raw signals.** I'd expect one of these:
- **Technical records (my best guess):** a table of transmitters with location, frequency, power, antenna and height. Traficom licenses radio use in Finland, so this would fit.
- **Measurements:** signal strength over time and frequency, which can be viewed as an image (a spectrogram).
- **Interference reports:** past cases, possibly as text. GPS disturbance is a known issue around the Baltic, but I don't know if it's in scope.

## How I'd solve it
The core question: **if a new transmitter is added, who gets disturbed, and which frequency or location avoids it?**

1. **Physics simulator:** the received interference is roughly transmit power + antenna gains − signal loss over distance, terrain and frequency. Free-space loss is the simple starting formula:
   `Loss (dB) = 92.45 + 20·log10(freq in GHz) + 20·log10(distance in km)`
   Real planning uses more detailed ITU propagation models, and we could add one if time allows.
2. **Generate training data:** create many random scenarios and calculate each one's interference level.
3. **Train the model:** input the scenario, output the interference level and a risk rating. If terrain maps are used, a small CNN could work; otherwise a small neural network or gradient boosting on the table is enough.
4. **Search for a better plan:** use the fast model to test thousands of frequency and location options, then re-check the best ones with the simulator.
5. **Demo:** a map of Finland with a risk heatmap that updates when you drag a transmitter or change its frequency, plus a "suggest a safer frequency" button.

**The honest test:** the model has to beat the plain formula, in speed or in accuracy against real data. If it can't do either, a physics tool with smart search may be the better product, even with less ML.

## Ask at the briefing
1. What data do we get: licence records, measurements or past interference cases?
2. Which frequency bands and systems matter most?
3. How do specialists check for interference today, and which step is slowest?
4. What interference level counts as a problem?
5. Is there real data we can test against?
6. What would you judge as a success: risk detection, planning suggestions or both?

If it's measurement data instead, the plan changes to detecting and classifying interference from spectrograms, and that's still model training.

## How it fits together

| Step | What happens | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| **1. City** | Build a 3D model from buildings and terrain | OpenStreetMap, plus open data from the City of Turku or the National Land Survey |
| **2. Satellites** | Calculate real satellite passes over Turku | Public orbit data (CelesTrak) and Skyfield |
| **3. Radio** | Trace how signals bounce off and get blocked by buildings | NVIDIA Sionna RT, a ray-tracing radio simulator |
| **4. Interference** | Add 5G masts and compare the unwanted signal with the wanted one | Our own code |
| **5. Dataset** | Run thousands of mast locations, frequencies and powers | Our laptops, maybe LUMI |
| **6. Model** | Train a U-Net: building map + transmitter → signal and risk map | PyTorch |
| **7. Demo** | Drag a mast, watch the interference map update, and see satellite passes | Web page |

**The model's value:** ray tracing a scenario takes far longer than a trained model would. That lets you test thousands of plans quickly, which fits Traficom's "more efficient spectrum planning". Others have done similar work (RadioUNet, for example), so the approach has a track record.

## Simplifications to make
- **Satellite signals:** don't trace them through space. A standard link budget gets the signal down to Turku, and only the last stretch through the city needs detail. Most of the interference story can stay on the ground.
- **The victim:** focus on one case, such as a 5G mast disturbing a satellite ground station. One finished case beats five half-done ones.
- **Materials:** give buildings simple material types, and state this openly as a limitation.

## Risks
- **Sim only:** results aren't proven real without real measurements. Ask Traficom for any data to check against.
- **Wrong problem:** Traficom might care about licence records, not city-level propagation. If the briefing goes that way, reuse the simulator as support and change the focus.
- **Hardware:** Sionna's fast GPU mode relies on NVIDIA. LUMI's GPUs are AMD, so simulations there may have to run on CPU, while LUMI's GPUs can still train the model. I need to confirm this.
- **Laptop memory:** 6 GB is tight, so keep the scenes small at first.
- **Scope:** this is the biggest risk. Have a basic version working by Saturday morning, even if it's rough.

The same idea can carry over to FORCIT, but it's a much weaker fit than Traficom. Everything here is my guess, because the real task stays secret until you've chosen the challenge and signed the NDA.

## What the twin could look like
A digital twin of a **quarry bench or tunnel face**: the rock, the drill holes and the charges.

1. **Simulate:** vary the hole pattern, explosive amount, timing and rock type.
2. **Calculate the results:** rock fragment size, ground vibration, flying rock risk and cost.
3. **Train:** teach a model to predict those results from a blast design.
4. **Optimise:** search thousands of designs for the best balance of safety and cost.
5. **Demo:** drag drill holes around in 3D and watch predicted vibration and fragmentation update.

## Why it's harder than Traficom

| | **Traficom** | **FORCIT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Simulator** | Ready-made tools like Sionna | I don't know of an equally easy tool; true blast physics is very hard to simulate |
| **Fast version** | Rough but workable physics | Mostly rough formulas like Kuz-Ram and scaled-distance |
| **Public data** | Maps and satellite orbits | Little, and hidden rock conditions matter a lot |
| **Fit known before choosing** | Reasonable | Unknown, as the title suggests the focus could be cycle operations instead |
| **Demo for voters** | Video allowed by default | The company can turn off the video and deck |

If the simulator is only those simple formulas, an ML model just copies them, which isn't impressive. For FORCIT, the better approach would probably be to **train on their real data** and use physics formulas as extra inputs or a sanity check. That could be a very good project, but it depends on what data they give you.

## When FORCIT would be the better pick
- The team wants the bigger prize (€3,000 for first) more than a likely shot at the finals.
- You're comfortable choosing without seeing the task.
- You accept that a private repo is safer and that no NDA data can leave the approved setup. Check whether you're even allowed to use outside AI tools, like Claude Code, on their data. The guide says not to send confidential data to outside AI providers without permission.

That last point matters a lot since your whole team plans to use Claude Code.

## My recommendation
**Keep Traficom first if you want the digital twin.** It's where your idea is strongest and the risk is easiest to manage. Keep FORCIT as a backup only if the whole team agrees to the unknowns, because the final choice locks in at selection.

**Sionna works, and it's fast enough for your idea.** It simulated radio signals through about 1 km² of real Kupittaa buildings on your laptop, in about half a second per map. The picture shows a 3.5 GHz signal from a test mast at 35 m: bright streets where the signal travels freely, and darker areas behind buildings.

Plugging in or unplugging mid-test may have affected some timings, but they're fast either way.

| Mode (200×200 map, 5 m cells) | Time per map | Area with signal |
|---|---|---|
| GPU, basic | 0.12 s | 34% |
| GPU, more rays and bounces | 0.15 s | 62% |
| **GPU, with signal bending around edges (diffraction)** | **0.5 s** | **83%** |
| CPU only, more rays and bounces | 0.6 s | 62% |

**What this means**
- **Dataset size:** at 0.5 s per map, 10,000 maps would take about 1.5 hours on your laptop, so the training data is realistic in the time you have.
- **LUMI:** CPU mode also ran fine here, so the simulation shouldn't depend on NVIDIA. I haven't tested it on LUMI itself.
- **Diffraction should stay on:** it's what fills in many of the shadowed areas. White areas in the picture are mostly building footprints or places no ray reached.

**What's still rough or untested**
- **Heights:** only 192 of the 336 buildings had height data, so I set the rest to 10 m.
- **Terrain:** the ground is flat for now, though real elevation data could be added.
- **Materials:** all buildings are treated as concrete.
- **Accuracy:** the results aren't checked against real measurements, so this shows it runs, not that it's right.
- **Not tried yet:** satellites, interference and training the model.

The test is outside your repo, and nothing was committed. The files are in `/tmp/claude-1000/-data-dev-sinceAI-hackathon/63bd467c-6630-4424-a1f2-7460e15f0fb4/scratchpad/sionna`, and that temporary folder may not last, so tell me if you want them saved elsewhere.

**For your team:** this makes Traficom a realistic first choice. A sensible next test is whether a small model can learn these maps from a few hundred simulations, and it should take less than an hour to find out. Want me to run that now, or is this enough for your team to decide?

content.text:
Here's the 3D scene of central Helsinki, about 1 km², which you can rotate and zoom: https://claude.ai/artifact/WSWJTt86Yw71cxkvmNE6ap

I couldn't open it myself, so I haven't seen it running. If it's blank or looks wrong, tell me what you see.

**What's in it**
- **Buildings:** 372 real buildings from OpenStreetMap.
- **Signal map:** the signal strength at street level, from weak to strong.
- **Ray paths:** the routes calculated by the simulator. Red lines go straight to the receiver, and yellow lines bounce off something along the way.
- **Masts:** 5 positions you can switch between with the buttons. You can also turn the rays, map and buildings on or off.

**This is a real simulation.** The ray tracing did the physics, and the 3D page just displays its results. Each signal map took about 0.5 s or less to calculate.

**What it can't do yet**
- **No live dragging:** those 5 positions are calculated ahead of time. Moving a mast anywhere would need a live backend or the trained model, which is really the reason to train one.
- **No satellites or interference yet:** so far it's one mast and its signal.
- **Rough assumptions:** 114 of the 372 buildings had no height data, so I set them to 10 m. The ground is flat, and every building is concrete.
- **Not checked against real measurements:** so the numbers aren't proven accurate yet.

**Helsinki or Turku?** Helsinki has more building height data (258 of 372, against 192 of 336 for Kupittaa) and taller buildings. I recall it also publishes a detailed open 3D city model, but I haven't checked that yet. Turku is where the event is, which could make a nicer story. Either can work, as the same steps ran for both.

If this is the kind of thing you pictured, the next step is adding a satellite pass and a second transmitter to show actual interference. Is this what you had in mind?
looks fine but it not impressive. I think we need to use some  sftware like Fluid dynamics use fo this.But what is the probelm we are solving i dont get it

Let's sort out the problem first, because that's what makes it impressive. A more detailed simulation alone won't.

## The problem we'd be solving
Radio frequencies are limited, and satellites and ground systems have to share them. Say a company wants to put up a new 5G mast near a satellite ground station. Traficom's specialists need to know:

1. **Will it disturb anything?**
2. **If so, what can change:** location, frequency, power or antenna direction?

Satellite signals arrive very weak, so a nearby mast can drown them out. Checking each option accurately takes time, so you can't test thousands of them.

**Our pitch:** *"Before a mast is approved, see in seconds what it would disturb, and get a safer option."*

That part about how specialists work today is my assumption, so it's the first thing to ask Traficom on Friday. If their real pain is something else, we change the project.

| Part | Its job |
|---|---|
| Simulation | Produces the training data |
| ML model | Gives near-instant answers |
| Search | Finds a safer plan |
| 3D twin | Makes it easy to understand |

## Would fluid-dynamics-style software help?
The radio equivalent exists: full wave solvers such as Meep or openEMS, which solve Maxwell's equations on a grid. **They won't work at city scale.** At 3.5 GHz the wavelength is about 8.6 cm, so a typical grid of 10 cells per wavelength across a 1 km cube needs about **1.6 quadrillion cells**. That's out of reach even for LUMI in a weekend.

Ray tracing is the standard tool at this scale, so what you've seen is already the right kind of simulator. A wave solver could still work for something tiny, like one antenna or one rooftop, and it would look great, but it wouldn't answer Traficom's question.

## What would make it impressive
It looks plain because it's static and nothing is at stake. I'd change that with:
1. **Live dragging:** move a mast and the risk map updates instantly. This is the moment people remember.
2. **A clear stake:** a satellite ground station turns from green to red with a warning.
3. **A real fix:** press "Find safer plan" and the system finds a frequency or position, and the station turns green again.
4. **Moving satellites:** real passes crossing the sky, with the risk changing over time.
5. **Before and after numbers:** for example, how long it takes to check thousands of options with the simulator versus the model, once we've measured both.

**The 20-second video:** a mast goes up, the station turns red, one click later it's green, and "10,000 options checked" appears.

Does that problem make sense to you? If the team isn't excited by it, it's better to know now, because the selection on Friday is final. I'd pick this one if at least a couple of you are keen on the radio side.
whatsba staelite ground staiton and what a mast

**A mast** is a tall pole or rooftop antenna that sends and receives radio signals over a local area. The most familiar kind is a mobile phone mast, the antennas you see on rooftops and towers. Your phone connects to the nearest one for calls and 5G.

**A satellite ground station** is a site on Earth with a dish antenna that talks to satellites in space. It's like a much bigger, more sensitive version of a satellite TV dish. These stations are used for things like downloading weather and Earth-observation images, or for communications.

**Why they can clash**

| | **Mast** | **Ground station** |
|---|---|---|
| **Signal source** | Close by and strong | From a satellite, hundreds or thousands of km away, so very weak |
| **Job** | Sends signals out to phones | Listens for faint signals from space |

It's like trying to hear someone whispering from far across a field while someone nearby is shouting. If the mast uses the same or a nearby frequency, its signal can drown out the satellite's. Then the station may lose some or all of the satellite's data.

**How the problem can be fixed:** move the mast, point its antenna another way, lower its power, or use a different frequency. Buildings between the two can also help by blocking the signal, which is why the 3D city model is useful.

So our demo in one line: **a new phone mast would disturb a satellite dish, and our tool spots it and suggests a fix.**

i feel like this will not work. I dont know a solution to this. Like impossible. im thinking of a new physics simulation similar to flouid dynamics but for radoii signals or 5g or 6g compared to the satelite signlas arriving

It isn't impossible, and you don't need to know the full solution yet. Your new idea is also a good one: **radio waves really can be simulated like fluid dynamics**, rippling through streets and around buildings. That method already exists and is called FDTD. We'd be building our own version for this use, not inventing new physics.

**The catch is size.** It can't cover a whole city, but a small area works:

| Area | Grid cells at 3.5 GHz | Doable? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 km, full 3D | About 1.6 quadrillion | No |
| 1 km, 2D | About 14 billion | Too big for a laptop |
| **50–100 m, 2D** | **About 35–140 million** | **Probably, in minutes to about an hour per run on your GPU (my estimate)** |

**What it could look like:** a side-on slice of a street, with buildings on it.
- The **satellite signal** comes down from above as weak, flat waves.
- The **5G or 6G mast** sends strong ripples outward from the side.
- You watch them **bounce, bend around corners and overlap**, and you can see the spot where the mast's waves swamp the satellite's.

This would be far more eye-catching than what I showed you, and it matches what you pictured. It could also make a great video.

**Where the AI comes in:** run many of these simulations with different streets and mast positions, then train a model to predict the result instantly. That's real physics-based ML, and it fits your training plan.

**The problem it solves stays the same:** *"Will this mast disturb the satellite signal here, and what would fix it?"* Now it just shows the answer far better, at street level. It complements the city map too: ray tracing covers the wide area, and the wave simulation zooms into one critical spot.

**The downsides:**
- **It's a slice:** 2D isn't the full real world, so we'd say that openly.
- **It's small:** it covers one street, not a whole city.
- **Traficom may want something else:** that's still the question for Friday's briefing.

You also don't have to decide this now. Want me to build a quick test so you can see the waves moving? It'd be a short animation on your GPU, kept outside your repo. If it looks exciting, you've got your project idea. If not, you've lost very little.
whts 3,.5ghz? whats 5g?

**3.5 GHz** is a frequency, which is how many times a radio wave vibrates per second.
- **Hz (hertz)** means vibrations per second.
- **GHz (gigahertz)** means billions per second, so 3.5 GHz is 3.5 billion vibrations per second.

Frequency also sets the wave's length. At 3.5 GHz, each wave is about **8.6 cm** long, roughly the width of a credit card.

Think of frequencies as **lanes on a motorway** or stations on a radio dial. Different services get their own lanes, and if two use the same lane in the same place, they can interfere. Traficom's job includes managing who uses which lanes in Finland.

| Frequency | Wave length | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Low** (like 700 MHz) | About 43 cm | Travels far and gets through walls better |
| **Medium** (like 3.5 GHz) | About 8.6 cm | A balance of speed and range |
| **High** (like 26 GHz) | About 1.2 cm | Very fast, short range, easily blocked |

**5G** is the fifth generation of mobile network technology, the system your phone uses for calls and internet. It's faster than 4G and can handle more devices at once. 5G is often run on frequencies around 3.5 GHz, which is why I used that number in the simulation.

**6G** is the planned next generation. It's still being developed, and new mobile generations need room on the radio dial, which can bring more sharing and more possible clashes with services like satellites.

**So, in plain words:** the simulation shows a 5G mast sending out waves about 8.6 cm long and how they travel around buildings.
surely we can do a 200 by 100 meter 3d

Sadly not at 3.5 GHz. A 200 × 100 m area with 50 m height sounds small, but the waves are only 8.6 cm long, so the grid gets enormous. It does become possible at a lower frequency if LUMI comes through. These are my rough estimates, using 10 cells per wavelength:

| 200 × 100 × 50 m in 3D | Grid cells | Memory | Where it could run |
|---|---|---|---|
| **3.5 GHz** (5G mid-band) | About 1.6 trillion | About 38 TB | Dozens of LUMI nodes and many hours, so not realistic |
| **700 MHz** (a lower 5G band) | About 13 billion | About 300 GB | **One LUMI GPU node, about 1–2 hours per run** |
| **About 190 MHz** | About 250 million | About 6 GB | Your laptop, only just |

**Why the jump is so big:** halving the frequency doubles the wave length, so you need half as many cells in each of the three directions. That's 8 times fewer cells overall.

**Best 3D option: 700 MHz on LUMI.**
- It's a real 5G frequency, with waves about 43 cm long.
- It would make a seriously impressive 3D visual: waves moving through real buildings.

**Three problems:**
1. **Your LUMI access isn't confirmed yet,** and this option depends on it. Also, nearly all of that one node's memory goes on this run.
2. **We couldn't produce many runs.** At 1–2 hours each, that's maybe a handful or a few dozen in the weekend, depending on how much LUMI time you get. That's enough for a stunning demo, but not enough to train a model on.
3. **The physics changes.** 700 MHz and 3.5 GHz behave differently around buildings, and satellite links often use other frequencies, so the results wouldn't directly answer a 3.5 GHz question.

**How I'd combine them:**
- **Training data:** thousands of fast 2D or ray-tracing runs. This is what teaches the model.
- **Showpiece:** one or two large 3D wave runs on LUMI for the video and to check that the faster methods are believable.

That gets you both the wow factor and the working AI.

**Next step:** a small test on your laptop, either the 2D street slice or a tiny 3D block, would show how the waves look and how fast they run on your GPU. That would replace my estimates with real numbers. Should I build it?
can i rent cloud gpu. Im happy to pay 20 euros for some good cloud gpu?

Yes, and €20 buys a useful amount of GPU time, but **I wouldn't spend it yet**. It won't get you the full 3D run at 3.5 GHz, and you may not need it at all.

**What €20 roughly gets** (prices from memory, so check before renting):

| GPU | Memory | Rough price | Time for €20 |
|---|---|---|---|
| RTX 4090 | 24 GB | €0.30–0.50/hour | 40–65 hours |
| A100 | 80 GB | €1–2/hour | 10–20 hours |
| H100 | 80 GB | €2–3/hour | 7–10 hours |

Vast.ai and RunPod are common places to rent by the hour. Stop the machine when you finish, as many charge while it's on, and some charge for storage even when it's stopped.

**What fits** (rough estimates):

| Simulation | Memory needed | Fits? |
|---|---|---|
| 3D, 200×100×50 m, 3.5 GHz | About 38 TB | No |
| 3D, 200×100×50 m, 700 MHz | About 300 GB | No, not on one GPU |
| 3D, 200×100×50 m, **about 450 MHz** | About 80 GB | A100/H100 |
| 3D, about **20×10×10 m**, 3.5 GHz | About 50 GB | A100/H100, a street corner rather than a block |
| 2D, 200×100 m, 3.5 GHz | About 3–4 GB | Yes, even your laptop's memory, but about an hour or more per run |

**Where rented GPUs help most**
- **Generating training data:** Sionna and small wave runs go faster, and you can run lots of them.
- **Training the model:** more memory and speed than your 6 GB laptop.
- **One beautiful 3D clip:** for the video, at a smaller size or a lower frequency.

**Free options to try first**
- **LUMI:** if approved, it costs you nothing and has much more GPU power.
- **Google Cloud's $300 trial:** it may cover GPUs, but new accounts often face restrictions, so check today if you want it as a backup.
- **Your laptop:** enough for the first test.

**My recommendation:** keep the €20 as a backup for the weekend. Run the small laptop test first to get real speed numbers, then rent only if you know what you'd use it for.

d="cuda"; f=3.5e9; lam=3e8/f; dx=lam/20; NX,NY=round(2/dx),round(1/dx); S=.5; T=lam/dx/S
print(NX,NY,"cells",NX*NY,"steps/period",T)
wall=torch.zeros(NX,NY,dtype=torch.bool,device=d)
def I(m): return round(m/dx)
wall[:,:I(.04)]=True                       # ground (y=0 bottom)
wall[I(.75):I(1.05),:I(.55)]=True          # building 1
wall[I(1.55):I(1.85),:I(.38)]=True         # building 2
pm=30; xx=torch.arange(NX,device=d).float(); yy=torch.arange(NY,device=d).float()

rx=(I(1.3),I(.08)); print("satellite-only power at dish",pa[rx],"with mast",pb[rx],"ratio dB",10*np.log10(pb[rx]/pa[rx]))

fig,ax=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(9,9.5))
ax[0].imshow(fa[-1],extent=[0,2,0,1]);ax[0].set_title("Satellite signal only (waves from above) — green = dish")
ax[1].imshow(fb[-1],extent=[0,2,0,1]);ax[1].set_title("Satellite + mast (yellow) — ripples spread, bounce and overlap")

I think I've also been making this harder than it needs to be. You said you felt lost, and I kept adding more physics and more options. A wave simulator isn't what you need right now, and neither is a decision tonight.

**You don't have to do Traficom.** It's only worth picking if someone on the team finds radio exciting, and it doesn't sound like that's you. Turku Energia or Europress are much easier to picture:
- **Turku Energia:** predict electricity use or prices for the next few hours, and show how sure the model is. You train a model on real data, and the graph explains itself.

**What I'd do now:** stop for today. Tomorrow, your team spends 10 minutes agreeing on three challenges, and your lead selects at 15:00. The real data arrives at 19:30, and that's when the actual solution gets worked out, so nobody is expected to know it yet.

like I thought we can make simulation preeeeety accurate and have real world physics and laws on how waves willl propgate around. Surely there stuff like that....

Yes, that software exists, and it's used for real network planning. Both things I showed you already use real wave physics; they were just quick versions with rough inputs and plain visuals, so they looked basic.

**The main tools** (from memory, so check licences and current features):

| Type | Tools | Scale | Accessible? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Exact wave physics** (Maxwell's equations) | Meep, openEMS, gprMax, Ansys HFSS | Antennas, rooms, small objects | Meep, openEMS and gprMax are free; HFSS is paid |
| **Ray tracing** (rays with reflection, diffraction and scattering) | **Sionna RT**, Remcom Wireless InSite, Altair WinProp | Streets to cities | Sionna is free; the others are paid |
| **Regulatory models** (standard formulas) | ITU-R P.452, P.1812 | Up to hundreds of km | Published standards |
| **Full digital twin with 3D visuals** | NVIDIA Aerial Omniverse Digital Twin | City | Needs serious NVIDIA hardware, likely rented |

**How accurate can it get?** The physics laws are already very accurate. The errors mostly come from what you feed in:
- **City model:** exact building shapes, heights, windows and trees.
- **Materials:** concrete and glass behave differently, and exact values are rarely known.
- **Antennas:** their real pattern and direction.
- **Changing conditions:** people, cars, rain and moving leaves.

Good ray tracing can get close to real measurements, often within several dB when calibrated, but no tool predicts every spot perfectly. The usual way to get accurate results is to **calibrate against real measurements**.

**The most realistic setup for us:** keep Sionna and improve its inputs:
1. Use a detailed 3D city model, such as Helsinki's open one if it suits, instead of plain blocks.
2. Assign real materials to buildings, with published ITU values.
3. Use real antenna patterns.
4. Ask Traficom for measurements to calibrate against.

Interference happens **at the dish**: if 5G energy reaches the dish on a frequency it's listening to, that energy mixes with the faint satellite signal. So the demo would show:
- **Satellites** moving across the sky, with the dish tracking one.

**Valmet is the best match so far for your digital twin and Omniverse idea.** Its summary talks about connecting the physical and digital worlds, and that's what a digital twin does. You own what you build, and Valmet can use it in its business.

**The problem:** the summary mentions understanding equipment, navigating environments and supporting field-service decisions. **A possible solution: an AI field assistant**
1. **Twin:** build a 3D model of a small industrial site, using Omniverse or similar.
2. **Generate training images:** render equipment from thousands of angles and lighting conditions, with automatic labels.
3. **Train:** teach a small vision model to recognise equipment and spot visible problems like leaks or damage.

content.text:
Written for: your 5-person team, to agree the plan.

**Yes, it's doable as a working demo inside a simulated factory floor.** Real-phone navigation inside a real plant isn't realistic in about 38 hours. None of this stack has been tested yet, so prove Isaac Sim first.

The full one-page version is here, private until you share it: https://claude.ai/artifact/W9aSYd24WVGe7tRSVpUZZn

| # | Feature | How it works | Tools | Doable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Factory twin** | One floor area with 5–10 machines, from Valmet's scan or a sample scene; machines come from sim assets or photos turned into 3D | Isaac Sim, OpenUSD, COLMAP or an image-to-3D tool | Yes, medium risk |
| 2 | **Machine detection** | Render labelled images in the sim, train the detector, then place each detection on a 3D map | Replicator, YOLO, PyTorch | Yes |
| 3 | **Voice assistant** | The worker asks by voice, and the LLM answers only from the database and manuals, showing its source | Whisper, LLM, text-to-speech, PostgreSQL, TimescaleDB, pgvector | Yes |
| 4 | **Route to machine** | A* finds a path on the twin's floor map and shows it in a phone web app, using the worker's position in the sim | Python, FastAPI, three.js | Yes |

**What I changed or added**
- **3D map:** Valmet's brief asks for "semantic 3D understanding", so detections need to become a labelled 3D map. YOLO alone won't cover that.
- **Valmet's scan:** the brief mentions scanned environments, so use their scan if they provide one.
- **Worker position:** a phone can't easily tell where it is inside a real plant, so the demo takes the position from the sim.
- **Database:** I assumed "tigerdb" means TimescaleDB, which runs inside PostgreSQL, so you'd only need one database. Please confirm that's what you meant.

**Biggest risks**
- **Isaac Sim setup:** it could eat the first night. Stop at 02:00 on Saturday and switch to Blender for images and three.js for the demo.
- **Too many parts:** have a basic version of all four connected by Saturday noon, then improve it.
- **Real photos:** a model trained on sim images may fail on them, so test on real ones early.
- **Licence and data:** Ultralytics YOLO is AGPL-3.0, so check that before using it. Also ask Valmet whether their data can go to a cloud LLM.

The RTX 5090 listed in `AGENTS.md` should run Isaac Sim, so you may not need to rent a GPU. It's shared, so check it's free first.
